analysis.title: Geopolitical turbulence complicates airlines' flight paths for 2027
key_insights: ING expects global air passenger growth to rebound to around 5% in 2027 in its base case, after about 1% in 2026 versus a structural 4-5%.

Jet fuel could account for close to 35% of airline operating costs in 2026, up from 27% in 2025. Tight refinery capacity and low inventories are likely to keep middle-distillate prices elevated well into 2027 even if oil eases.

European airline fuel hedges (40-90% of consumption) roll off progressively through 2027, so European fares have further to rise. US airlines hedge less and have already passed costs through to fares.
Low-cost carriers are most exposed because fuel is a larger share of their costs and price-sensitive passengers limit fare pass-through. Premium carriers can raise fares with less demand loss.

Middle East traffic halved in March and April 2026 and was still 15% lower y/y in August. The region was 9.5% of global RPKs, and the setback cut an estimated 2-3 percentage points from global growth.

European carriers such as Lufthansa and Air France-KLM benefited from traffic shifting away from Middle Eastern hubs. Europe-Asia traffic was up more than 12% y/y in August, while Middle East-Asia was down almost 12%.
Airbus and Boeing had a combined backlog of around 15,000 aircraft by mid-2026. Scarcity keeps aircraft values and lease rates high and forces airlines to fly older, less efficient planes.

Boeing plans to raise 737 MAX production from 38 to 47 a month and recently received certification for the 737 MAX 7 and MAX 10. This should support 2027 deliveries and helps Boeing-dependent airlines such as Ryanair and Southwest.

Industry operating margins are expected to fall meaningfully below 5%, a post-pandemic low. Ryanair, Southwest and AirAsia have cut capacity on unprofitable routes, and Cirium says about 1% of global capacity will be removed for winter 2026-27.
Industry headwinds could prompt consolidation, from minority stakes to full takeovers.

Air cargo volume is up almost 5% year-to-date with attractive freight rates, supported by high-value technology and AI-related shipments. European carriers also gained from reduced Middle Eastern freight capacity.

Asia's share of the global aircraft fleet is expected to rise from about 33% to about 45%. India's fleet could grow about 8% a year over the next two decades, backed by large IndiGo and Air India orders.
Ticket prices are unlikely to return to early-2026 levels even if fuel falls, given resilient demand, limited aircraft supply and general inflation.
European airlines face added costs from the EU ETS and the ReFuelEU SAF mandate, which together add about $300 per tonne of jet fuel in 2026. Several countries are changing ticket taxes.

sector_views.rationale: Fuel is a larger share of costs, hedges roll off in 2027, and price-sensitive passengers limit fare pass-through.
More pricing power in premium cabins. United and Delta reported little demand impact after 15-20% price increases in Q2-Q3.
Volume up almost 5% YTD with attractive rates, supported by technology and AI-related shipments and reduced Middle Eastern capacity.

earnings_insights: Ryanair is about 80% hedged until Q2 2027 and has warned of significantly higher fares.
United Airlines and Delta Air Lines reported little demand impact after fare increases of 15-20% in Q2 to Q3 2026.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Well below the structural 4-5%, driven by the Middle East disruption and fuel cost shock.

tension_points.bull_case: Resilient demand, high load factors, limited aircraft supply and premium-cabin pricing power let airlines raise fares. United and Delta saw little impact after 15-20% increases.
tension_points.bear_case: Price-sensitive low-cost passengers limit pass-through, European hedges roll off in 2027, and some demand destruction has already occurred.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Fuel prices easing in 2027 could let fares drop back, though ING does not expect a return to early-2026 levels.

theme_stances.key_argument: Tight refinery capacity and low inventories keep jet fuel elevated into 2027 even if oil eases, and European hedges expire.
theme_stances.evidence: Tight refinery capacity and low inventories are likely to keep prices elevated

theme_stances.key_argument: Backlog and slow deliveries keep capacity tight and support aircraft values, while Boeing production is recovering.
theme_stances.evidence: Aircraft shortages will continue to constrain capacity.
